A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same tensor-equivariance framework and sparse-vector application, despite the changed title and expanded scope. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix H report original sparse-vector-recovery experiments, including test and training results across sampling distributions and covariance settings.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendices H–J report original stress–strain, path-signature, and retained sparse-vector experiments. The TFENN comparison scores are explicitly attributed to prior work.

M1.justification: v2 adds a distinct symmetric-matrix architecture: decompose the input into eigenvalues and eigenvectors, process the eigenvalues with a permutation-equivariant network, and reconstruct the output matrix (Corollary 2; Appendix H.2). The existing sparse-vector models and spectral estimation procedure are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds Neo-Hookean stress-from-strain prediction and synthetic polynomial-path signature estimation, including three-dimensional orthogonal and four-dimensional Lorentz settings (Section 5; Appendices H–I). The four sparse-vector sampling families and three covariance settings remain.

E2.justification: New comparisons include TFENN using published scores, augmentation-trained MLPs, a discrete path-signature estimator, and MLPs matched by width or parameter count (v2 Tables 1–2). The sparse-vector comparators remain; combining their identical SoS test scores into one column does not remove a method.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce substantial protocols: stress–strain training at three dataset sizes with 4,000 validation/test samples and 1,500 epochs; path signatures with 1,024 trajectories per split, ten input points, signatures through order three, and 500 epochs. They introduce Frobenius-error metrics and augmentation controls. The reported sparse-vector training protocol is substantially retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds a limited training-data-size sensitivity comparison for stress–strain prediction, evaluating 5,000, 20,000, and 40,000 samples (Table 1). The existing sparse-vector full-versus-diagonal comparison, covariance analyses, and training-versus-test evidence are retained.

E5.justification: Sparse-vector results retain five-trial means and standard deviations. The new path-signature comparison specifies three trials and reports standard deviations only when they reach 0.001 (Table 2), introducing a different reporting rule. Stress–strain results otherwise follow the existing five-trial reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for both new tasks: for example, stress–strain error of 4.057e-6 with 5,000 training samples, and path-signature errors of 0.002 and 0.005 for orthogonal and Lorentz settings (Tables 1–2). Sparse-vector numerical test and training results match v1 after accounting for renamed columns and merged identical SoS scores.

T1.justification: v2 adds the symmetric-matrix characterization in Corollary 2, with a simultaneous-diagonalization lemma and proof in Appendix F, plus an explicit computational-complexity bound in Section 3. It also corrects mathematical expressions, including the missing Kronecker delta in Example 1. The principal general tensor and other-group theorems are retained.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes learning spectral algorithms for sparse-vector recovery. v2 reframes the empirical contribution around a general tensor-learning recipe demonstrated across materials science, path signatures, and sparse recovery, and explicitly claims novelty at this level of generality. The underlying characterization of orthogonal, Lorentz, and symplectic equivariance remains.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit discussion of practical output-order limits and memory costs relative to Clebsch–Gordan methods. It removes v1's discussion of joint permutation invariance and its graph-isomorphism difficulty, as well as the suggestion that learned sparse-vector algorithms could generate theoretical conjectures. The principal interpretation of the sparse-vector results remains.

D1.justification: New Appendices H–I document dataset access, path generation with Signax, normalization, augmentation, network sizes, optimizer schedules, hardware, and training time. Appendix J.4 additionally specifies covariance selection per experimental trial. The original repository link and most sparse-vector implementation details are retained.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against e3nn, escnn, Domina et al., and Pearce-Crump, explaining differences between invariant-theory and representation-theory constructions. It adds materials and path-signature literature while removing the earlier neural-algorithmic-reasoning framing and associated references. These changes exceed bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Section 3 gains explanatory guidance and reordered exposition; the isotropic-tensor lemma moves to Appendix C. Much of the sparse-vector setup and model description moves into Appendix J, allowing the main experiments section to cover three applications.

P2.justification: v2 adopts conference typography, headers, and table styling; adds the explanatory architecture diagram in Figure 1 and four tables for new results and settings; and restructures retained tables. The sparse-vector test table merges identical SoS columns, and its parameter table changes orientation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the connection between the general theory and practical tensor learning. The proved symmetric-matrix construction and new experiments demonstrate matrix inputs, higher-order outputs, and Lorentz equivariance beyond v1's sole sparse-vector application. Parameter-matched and augmentation comparisons strengthen the empirical evidence, while detailed appendices improve reproducibility. Some earlier limitations discussion is lost, and TFENN scores are imported rather than rerun, but these qualifications do not outweigh the substantial gains.
